1352.title: The Miraculous Medal (1830)
1352.hook: Catherine Labouré's vision in Paris: O Mary, conceived without sin
1352.howItsDone: Catholics wear the Miraculous Medal on a chain or carry it, often blessed by a priest, and say its short prayer, "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee."

segments.voice: Yesterday, Totus Tuus: a whole life handed over in two Latin words. Your line was totally yours.

A small oval of stamped metal, on a thin chain, tucked under a nurse's scrubs. Pressed into the palm of someone in a hospital bed by a grandmother who says, just keep it. On the back, a whole picture: a letter, a cross, two hearts, a ring of stars. On the front, a woman with light pouring from her hands, and a line of words around the edge. And the design wasn't dreamed up by a jeweler. It came from a young woman's account of one night in Paris.
screen: `A SMALL OVAL ON A CHAIN.` → `TWO HEARTS AND A RING OF STARS.` → `WHERE DID THE DESIGN COME FROM?`

segments.voice: First, the vision. Catherine was a young novice with the Daughters of Charity in Paris. By her own account, Mary appeared to her standing on a globe, with rays of light streaming from her hands, an oval of words around her. Then it turned to show the back, and she was told to have a medal struck after that model. Her confessor was cautious, but the medal was made, and the story goes that Catherine told almost no one it was her, and spent her years quietly caring for old men in a hospice. Second, the words on the front: "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee." That's the Immaculate Conception, which you met back in year one: the Church teaches that Mary, from the first moment of her life, was kept free from original sin, by the grace of her son. It's about Mary's beginning, not Jesus's birth. A later pope defined it as dogma, and the medal's admirers note that its words said it first. Third, the back. A letter M with a cross rising out of it. Below, two hearts: one ringed with thorns, for Jesus, and one pierced by a sword, for Mary. Around them, twelve stars, which readers connect to the woman in the Apocalypse, in the Douay-Rheims: "on her head a crown of twelve stars." Fourth, the name. People called it miraculous because of the cures and conversions they reported. The Church is careful: a medal isn't a charm, and it does nothing by itself. It's a reminder you can wear.
screen: `A NOVICE IN PARIS, A VISION AT NIGHT.` · `O MARY, CONCEIVED WITHOUT SIN.` · `AN M, A CROSS, TWO HEARTS, TWELVE STARS.` · `NOT A CHARM: A REMINDER YOU WEAR.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR US WHO HAVE RECOURSE TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Hold a medal, or whatever you carry close, a ring, a cross, a key, and let it stand for someone you'd like to keep close today. If you pray, say the medal's line slowly: O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee; if not, simply hold the object, and the person, and breathe.
The Miraculous Medal. The medal from Saint Catherine's account in Paris: Mary's prayer around the front, an M, a cross, two hearts and twelve stars on the back. Today's word.
Your line: conceived without sin. Mary's beginning, kept whole by grace. Rest well.

1353.title: May crowning
1353.hook: children crown a statue of Mary with flowers in May
1353.howItsDone: Some Catholic parishes and schools hold a May crowning in spring: children bring flowers in procession, one child places a crown of flowers on a statue of Mary, and the people sing Marian hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Miraculous Medal: a prayer stamped in metal, worn close. Your line was conceived without sin.

The procession is already moving down the aisle. Children in their best clothes, some still in first Communion white, each holding a few flowers: grocery-store tulips, lilacs cut from somebody's backyard, one dandelion held very seriously by a small boy. The flowers are laid at the feet of a statue of Mary until there's a small hill of them. Then one child climbs a step and sets a ring of flowers on the statue's head. People sing. Somebody's phone is out. And for a moment the whole parish is looking at a child's hands.
screen: `CHILDREN, FLOWERS, A PROCESSION.` → `A HILL OF FLOWERS AT HER FEET.` → `ONE CHILD LIFTS THE CROWN.`

segments.voice: You met this one briefly, among the months and their themes. First, what it is. A May crowning is a popular devotion, not a required feast. Parishes and schools hold one in the spring, often in May, the month Catholic custom gives to Mary: flowers for a mother, in the season of flowers. Second, why a child. In Matthew's Gospel, children in the temple are shouting hosanna, and the chief priests are annoyed. Jesus answers them with a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "Out of the mouth of infants and of sucklings thou hast perfected praise." The crowning puts that verse into practice. The grown-ups could do it more neatly; they hand it to a child anyway. Third, why flowers and not gold. Jesus points to the lilies of the field and says, "not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed as one of these." A crown of flowers is cheaper than a king's, and in that saying it outshines one. Catholics call Mary queen because her son is king, and the Council speaks of her exalted by the Lord as queen. But the crown a parish gives her grows in backyards. Fourth, the line. Some readers trace the title queen of the May to old spring festivals where a girl was crowned with flowers, and a hymn sung at some crownings calls Mary queen of the angels and queen of the May in one breath. By week's end, the crown will be brown and drooping, and someone will quietly take it down. The gift doesn't have to last to be given.
screen: `A DEVOTION, NOT A DUTY.` · `OUT OF THE MOUTH OF INFANTS.` · `NOT EVEN SOLOMON IN ALL HIS GLORY.` · `A CROWN THAT WILTS, GIVEN ANYWAY.` · then, large: `QUEEN OF THE MAY.`

If you pray, offer it to Mary with the opening of the Hail Mary, Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; if not, simply offer it to someone you'd like to honor, and let it be enough.
May crowning. A spring devotion where a child sets a crown of flowers on a statue of Mary, and the parish sings. Today's word.

1354.title: Mary and Protestants
1354.hook: Protestants honor Mary in their own ways; Luther wrote a commentary on the Magnificat
1354.howItsDone: Catholics sing or say the Magnificat at Vespers, the Church's evening prayer; Anglicans sing it at Evening Prayer (Evensong) from the Book of Common Prayer, and Lutherans also use it at evening services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the May crowning: a child, a statue, a ring of flowers that wilts by week's end. Your line was queen of the may.

"My soul doth magnify the Lord." Late in the afternoon, in an old English cathedral, a choir in white robes stands to sing those words. It's Evensong, the evening prayer of the Church of England, and the words are Mary's. The same evening, in a Catholic monastery, monks sing the same song at Vespers, in Latin, beginning Magnificat. Two buildings, two churches, one young woman's song rising at dusk. People sometimes assume Mary belongs only to Catholics and the Orthodox, and that Protestants leave her out. The evening tells a more interesting story.
screen: `MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.` → `EVENSONG AND VESPERS, AT DUSK.` → `THE SAME SONG IN TWO CHURCHES.`

segments.voice: You learned Mary's song back in year one. First, the song itself. In Luke's Gospel, Mary visits her cousin Elizabeth and answers her greeting with a song. In the Douay-Rheims: "for behold from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed." Luke is in Catholic and Protestant Bibles alike, so calling Mary blessed is scripture. Second, Martin Luther. The same reformer who broke with Rome wrote a whole commentary on the Magnificat. He held it up as a lesson in how God looks on the lowly: Mary, a girl of no standing, chosen and lifted up, and the proud scattered. In it, Luther calls her the Mother of God. Third, the prayer book. The Church of England's Book of Common Prayer sets the Magnificat in Evening Prayer, so Anglicans sing at dusk: "My soul doth magnify the Lord : and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." Fourth, the honest differences. Catholics and Orthodox Christians ask Mary to pray for them, and Catholics hold teachings about her, like the Immaculate Conception, that Protestant churches don't share. Protestant churches differ among themselves too: some keep feasts of Mary; some honor her as a model of faith and listening, and pray to God without asking for her prayers. The Second Vatican Council spoke with joy of other Christians who honor the Mother of the Lord. So Mary isn't only a fence line. She's a place where people who disagree about a great deal still sing the same words.
screen: `ALL GENERATIONS SHALL CALL ME BLESSED.` · `LUTHER WROTE ON HER SONG.` · `EVENSONG: MARY'S SONG AT DUSK.` · `WHERE CHURCHES DIFFER, AND WHERE THEY MEET.` · then, large: `MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say slowly, the way choirs do at dusk: "My soul doth magnify the Lord." Breathe, and then: "And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." If you don't pray, simply hold the picture of two churches across a city, the same song going up from both at evening, and let the people in them be neighbors for a minute.
Mary and Protestants. Churches that differ about Mary, still singing her song: Luther's commentary, the prayer book's Evensong, the Magnificat in Catholic and Protestant Bibles alike. Today's word.
Your line: she belongs to all. One song, sung at dusk in more than one church. I'll be here tomorrow.

1355.title: The Dormition
1355.hook: the Orthodox call the August feast of Mary her falling asleep
1355.tomorrow: Mary close: do whatever he tells you
1355.howItsDone: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians keep the feast of the Dormition with the Divine Liturgy and a fast beforehand; in the West, Catholics keep the same day as the Assumption, which in some countries is a holy day of obligation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary and Protestants: one song, sung at dusk in more than one church. Your line was she belongs to all.

Look closely at the icon. Mary lies on a low bed, eyes closed, hands folded. Around her stand the apostles, bent with grief. One leans down close to her face; others hold their hands to their cheeks. Behind the bed, taller than everyone, stands Christ, in light. In his arms he holds a small figure wrapped in white, like a newborn. That small figure is Mary's soul. Think of the Christmas icons: a mother holding her swaddled child. Here it's turned around. The son holds his mother, swaddled, and carries her home. Orthodox Christians have a name for this feast, and it isn't death.
screen: `MARY ON A LOW BED, APOSTLES GRIEVING.` → `CHRIST HOLDS A SMALL SWADDLED FIGURE.` → `THE SON CARRIES HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: You met the Assumption back in year one. First, the name. Orthodox Christians call the feast the Koimesis, the falling asleep; in Latin, Dormition. It's the feast the Latin Church calls the Assumption, and Eastern Catholics keep it as the Dormition too. Second, why sleep. The New Testament uses that word for the death of the faithful. When Stephen is stoned, the Douay-Rheims says that, having prayed for the men killing him, "he fell asleep in the Lord." Paul writes to the Thessalonians about those who are asleep, so they won't grieve like people without hope. You only call it sleep if you expect a waking. Third, the story. The Bible doesn't tell how Mary's life ended. Tradition says the apostles were gathered to her bedside, that she was laid in a tomb, and that her body was not left there. The icon comes from that tradition, not from a Gospel, and the Church keeps the two apart. Fourth, two names for one hope. The Catholic Church teaches, as dogma, that Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory. Notice the phrasing: Pius the Twelfth defined the Assumption without deciding whether she died first. The Catechism quotes an Eastern hymn about her falling asleep. The Orthodox speak plainly of her death, and of her son taking her to himself. One tradition names the arrival, the other the moment of closing her eyes. Both point at the same door.
screen: `KOIMESIS: THE FALLING ASLEEP.` · `HE FELL ASLEEP IN THE LORD.` · `THE STORY COMES FROM TRADITION.` · `ONE HOPE, TWO NAMES.` · then, large: `TAKEN UP, BODY AND SOUL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind an Orthodox church you've passed, an Orthodox Christian you know, or simply the candles lit before icons tonight, and hold them a few breaths with good will. If you pray, use a short Byzantine refrain on the out-breath, most holy Mother of God, save us. If you don't, simply hold the picture: a son carrying his mother, gently, the way she once carried him.
Dormition. The falling asleep: the Eastern name for the end of Mary's earthly life, the feast the West calls the Assumption. Today's word.
Your line: fell asleep. The Bible's old word for death, said with hope. Until tomorrow.

1356.title: Mary close: do whatever he tells you
1356.hook: every Marian title points back to her son
1356.howItsDone: Catholics read the wedding at Cana in the Mass and pray it as a Luminous Mystery of the rosary, and Catholic writers quote Mary's words to the servants when they explain devotion to her.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dormition: an icon of a son carrying his mother home. Your line was fell asleep.

A wedding in Cana, a village in Galilee, and the party is going well, until the wine runs out. For the bride and groom, this is a disaster in front of everyone they know. The guests haven't noticed yet. The steward hasn't noticed. One guest has. Mary goes to her son and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." He answers with something that sounds like a gentle refusal. She doesn't argue. She turns to the servants instead, and what she tells them closes these days on Mary.
screen: `A WEDDING IN CANA.` → `THE WINE RUNS OUT.` → `THEY HAVE NO WINE.`

segments.voice: You heard this story in year one; today, watch Mary. First, she notices. Nobody asked her to watch the wine. She sees a need in somebody else's house and carries it straight to her son. That's the picture Catholics have when they ask her to pray for them: someone who notices what's running out, and takes it to him. Second, she steps aside. Her words to the servants, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Not do what I say: do what he says. Then she's out of the story. The servants fill the stone jars with water, carry some to the steward, and it's wine, the good wine, saved for last. Some readers notice that John's Gospel gives her no more lines after this; if so, her last words in it are an instruction to listen to someone else. Third, every title. Mother of God, because of who her son is. Ever virgin, a life kept for him. Conceived without sin, by his grace. The new Eve beside the new Adam. Queen, because he is king. Taken up, because he rose first. The tilma, where she carries him. Lourdes and Fatima, where the message is pray. The Catechism puts it in one line: what Catholics believe about Mary rests on what they believe about Christ. Every name points past her. Fourth, what comes next. Tomorrow the path turns east, to the churches that pray in Greek, Arabic, Syriac and Slavonic and still stand with Rome. Mary comes along, under the name the East gives her: Theotokos, the one who bore God.

1357.title: One Church, twenty-four churches
1357.hook: the Latin Church and the Eastern Catholic churches, all in communion with Rome
1357.howItsDone: Eastern Catholics belong to their own churches sui iuris, with their own bishops, liturgy and law, while in full communion with the pope; Latin Catholics may attend their liturgies, and in some cities Eastern Catholic parishes stand a few streets from Latin ones.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the close of the days on Mary, at a wedding where the wine ran out. Your line was she points to him.

A few streets from a parish with pews and a kneeler in every row, there's another church. Golden domes. Inside, a wall of icons, a cloud of incense, a priest with a beard, candles burning in front of the icons. The bulletin is in English and Ukrainian. A Catholic from the first parish walks in, a little unsure, and asks the woman at the door whether this is an Orthodox church. She smiles; she gets asked that a lot. No, she says. We're Catholic. We just aren't Roman.
screen: `DOMES, ICONS, INCENSE.` → `IS THIS ORTHODOX?` → `CATHOLIC, JUST NOT ROMAN.`

segments.voice: You met one of these churches, the Ukrainian Greek Catholics, earlier on this path. First, the phrase. Sui iuris is Latin for of its own law. The Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches uses it for a church with its own hierarchy, recognized as self-governing by the Church's highest authority: its own bishops, sometimes its own patriarch, its own law, liturgy, calendar, saints and ways of praying. And all of it in full communion with the bishop of Rome. Second, the families. The Catechism names the great liturgical traditions in the Church: the Latin, and then the Byzantine, the Alexandrian or Coptic, the Syriac, the Armenian, the Maronite and the Chaldean. Out of them come the Eastern Catholic churches: Ukrainians and Melkites, Maronites in Lebanon, Syro-Malabar Catholics in India, Chaldeans from Iraq, Copts, Ethiopians, Armenians and more. Third, equal dignity. The Second Vatican Council, in its decree on the Eastern churches, said these churches are of equal dignity, and that none outranks another because of its rite. The Latin Church sits at that table as one church among them, not the owner of the house. The Council asked the Eastern churches to keep their own traditions whole, not trade them for Latin ones. Fourth, the picture. Pope John Paul the Second wrote that the Church must breathe with both its lungs, East and West. Catholic doesn't only mean Roman. For a Latin Catholic, the parish with the domes isn't a stranger's church. It belongs to the same communion.

1358.title: The Byzantine churches
1358.hook: Ukrainian, Melkite, Ruthenian, Romanian and more pray in the Byzantine tradition
1358.howItsDone: Byzantine Catholics celebrate the Divine Liturgy, sung throughout, with icons and incense; they make the sign of the cross from the right shoulder to the left, and Latin Catholics may attend and receive communion there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sui iuris: of its own law, a family of churches inside one Church. Your line was one church, many churches.

Watch the hand. The thumb and the first two fingers press together at the tips. The last two fold down into the palm. Then the hand goes to the forehead, to the chest, to the right shoulder, and then the left. A Latin Catholic touches the left shoulder first. Three fingers joined, they say, for the Trinity; two folded, for the two natures of Christ, God and man. It's a small thing, a sign of the cross going the other way. And that hand belongs to a Catholic, praying in a tradition with long habits of its own.
screen: `THREE FINGERS JOINED, TWO FOLDED.` → `RIGHT SHOULDER, THEN LEFT.` → `A CATHOLIC HAND.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Byzantine comes from Byzantium, the old name of the city later called Constantinople. The way of worship that grew up there, its liturgy, chant, icons and calendar of feasts, carried the city's name with it, and the Catechism lists the Byzantine among the Church's great liturgical traditions. Second, the churches. Several Eastern Catholic churches pray in this tradition, each its own church sui iuris: Ukrainian Greek Catholics; Melkites, whose home is in Syria, Lebanon and the Holy Land, and who pray in Arabic and Greek; Ruthenians, from the Carpathian mountains; Romanian Greek Catholics; and others. Different languages, different histories, the same shape of prayer. Third, the neighbors. The Byzantine Catholic liturgy is, for the most part, the liturgy of the Orthodox churches: the same prayers, the same icons, often the same music. The difference isn't in the incense; it's in communion. Byzantine Catholics are in full communion with the bishop of Rome, and name the pope in their prayers. They stand close to their Orthodox neighbors and close to Rome at the same time, and that place in between hasn't always been an easy one to hold. Fourth, the open door. The Church's law says a Catholic keeps the Sunday obligation by attending Mass in any Catholic rite. So a Latin Catholic can walk into a Byzantine Catholic church on Sunday, stand through a liturgy in another shape, receive communion from a spoon, and be welcome. Same Church. Different room.
